This paper introduces a multimodal benchmark dataset for detecting frames and potential greenwashing in oil and gas video advertisements on Facebook and YouTube. The dataset consists of 691 videos annotated with 13 frame types (e.g., environment, community, green innovation), covering more than 50 companies across 21 countries.

The benchmark evaluates the capabilities of SOTA visual language models (VLMs) under zero-shot and one-shot settings, highlighting key challenges, including the detection of implicit frames, the analysis of short-form video content, and the influence of cultural variation. The dataset supports multiple applications, such as automatic greenwashing detection, temporal trend analysis, and broader investigations of corporate climate messaging.

Strengths
- First multimodal benchmark targeting framing and greenwashing detection in oil and gas advertising.
- Expert-annotated dataset of 691 videos spanning 21 countries and 50+ companies.
- Rigorous evaluation of VLMs on this new video classification task.
- Useful resource for greenwashing detection, trend analysis, and corporate profiling.

Weaknesses
- Limited label accuracy, particularly for the Facebook subset, where labels rely on ad text rather than video content.
- Class imbalance, with certain labels (e.g., "Patriotism", "Green Innovation") appearing infrequently.
- Dataset scale and coverage remain relatively limited compared to broader multimodal corpora.

Despite these limitations, the reviewers agree that the paper makes a valuable contribution by providing the first benchmark dataset for analyzing corporate greenwashing strategies in multimodal advertising. 
The rebuttal successfully addressed concerns, and no ethical issues were identified.

Reviewer Ctos, thank you so much for giving comments on dataset limitations. Reviewer daNe, thank you for pointing out dataset and modality concerns. Reviewer Reviewer AYF5, I appreciate your review and reply to our rebuttal. 

We acknowledged the limitations of the dataset and endeavored to clarify them as much as possible. We believe most of the reviewers concerns will be resolved in the revised manuscript.

As a final remark, we are pleased that all reviewers recognized the novelty of this study. We would like to emphasize that, as Reviewer AYF5 mentioned, our strength is grounded by a novel and timely multimodal dataset designed to analyze framing in corporate oil & gas (O&G) video ads. We hope our work can be a significant contribution to the field of climate change and AI communities.

We thank you for your insightful feedback on our paper. We recognize that your concerns are mainly about annotation clarification and dataset limitations. We address your comments as much as possible. Please find the following details.


> While the dataset construction and labeling process is discussed and grounded in prior work, the paper would benefit from including representative examples to illustrate the label definitions in more detail, helping readers better understand the annotation criteria.

Thank you for your comment. We agree that it is important to provide annotation examples in the paper to help readers understand the annotation criteria. We will incorporate some examples into the appendix in the revised version.


> There are two notable limitations in the Facebook subset: (i) approximately 55\% of the videos lack transcripts, reducing the effectiveness of multimodal analysis; and (ii) the data is geographically limited to the United States, which may restrict the generalizability and global relevance of the findings derived from this subset.

For limitation (i), it is true that approximately 55\% of the videos lack transcripts. However, we believe that the lack of transcripts serves as good motivation to address different modality (especially image frames) in benchmarking. Additionally, handling both videos with transcripts and those without can be an extra challenge for models. We will further detail this challenge in the revised version of the paper.



For limitation (ii), we acknowledge that geographical generalizability will be limited in the Facebook domain. In fact, campaign styles may differ across various communities. We would like to leave the extension to additional countries for future work.


We sincerely thank you for your feedback. If you have any concerns or additional comments, please feel free to let us know.

We thank you for your thoughtful review of our paper. We appreciate your comments on the dataset and models. We now address your concerns as much as possible. Please find the following details:

> Although the proposed dataset is a valuable contribution in the multimodal domain, its overall scale (692 videos) remains limited compared to prior text-only benchmarks. The relatively small dataset size raises concerns about potential overfitting during fine-tuning, which may partly explain why the authors focus exclusively on zero-shot and one-shot evaluations. This limitation could affect the model’s generalization capability in real-world scenarios.

Your comment on "partly explain why the authors focus exclusively on zero-shot and one-shot evaluations" is accurate. We acknowledge the limitation of our dataset size, although we believe our dataset is a significant contribution to the community. Please see our reply to Reviewer Rdgb for a more detailed discussion of the dataset size. We will certainly include this limitation and discussion in the revised version. 

Regarding your concern about the effects on model generalization in real-world scenarios, we will discuss this further in the limitations section of the revised version.

> While the motivation for a multimodal framework is clear, the absence of unimodal baselines (e.g., text-only classification results) makes it difficult to assess the specific contribution of each modality to the overall performance. Including such comparisons would strengthen the empirical analysis, help validate the added value of the multimodal approach, and substantiate the necessity of constructing a multimodal dataset for this task.

Thank you for pointing this out. We actually found it difficult to provide a fair comparison for the text-only models. This is because many videos do not contain any transcript text at all. For example, on Facebook, out of 306 videos, only 135 videos contain transcripts. 
Nevertheless, we provide a unimodal model for image frames. That is, we provide the ablation study with the non-transcript model in Table 3 and Appendix Table 7. These suggest that the transcript text input is important for Facebook. We believe this further strengthens the need for constructing a multimodal dataset for this task.

> Despite the use of expert annotations, certain framing categories (e.g., "Green Innovation" vs. "Environment") may suffer from semantic overlap and subjective interpretation. This potential ambiguity may introduce additional uncertainty in model evaluation, particularly when assessing fine-grained framing categories.

It is true that we encounter subjective interpretation and semantic overlap when labeling, even though we invested days of effort discussing the interpretation and resolving disagreements. We discuss the process to reduce ambiguity in Appendix A.5.4. Since we also report inter-annotator agreement for YouTube annotations, it is possible to estimate some of the uncertainty in model evaluation. However, we will include further discussion and limitations regarding this issue in the revised version of the paper.



We sincerely thank you for your feedback. If you have any concerns or additional comments, please feel free to let us know.

We thank you for the insightful feedback on our paper. We carefully read your comments on the limitations and weaknesses, and found that we can revise our paper by addressing your suggestions. Please find the details below:

> Limited label accuracy (especially for the Facebook subset) Facebook videos are labeled based on ad text rather than the overall content of the video. This “distant annotation” approach may ignore visual and tone cues in the video, reduce annotation quality, and bias model training and evaluation.

As you pointed out, the labels of Facebook videos are distantly annotated based on the text content. We acknowledge this limitation and discuss the quality of these distant labels in Appendix A.5.2: our small analysis found that the F-score between the original distant labels and our manual video-based annotations is 83\%. We cannot conclude whether this is sufficient, but at least we can roughly estimate the quality of the labels.
We will further discuss the limitation that visual and tone cues may be ignored and that bias may arise, in the revised version of this paper.


> Difficulty identifying implicit expressions and cultural differences Many “green” messages in videos are conveyed through metaphors and symbolic images (such as wind power generation, laboratories, etc.) and lack explicit language descriptions. Current models are weak in handling these implicit frames and cross-cultural expression differences (such as Asia vs. North America).

As you pointed out, cultural differences affect how implicit messages are conveyed. This applies not only to "green," but also to labels related to Patriotism and Community \& Life. In fact, videos from some cultures were particularly difficult to annotate. For example, in a video from a company showing people cooking and eating, implicit messages were conveyed even though there were no language descriptions. Conversely, language descriptions were often highly context-dependent. For example, "We are [Some Nationality]>" (Patriotism).

These highlight the importance of understanding diverse cultural backgrounds in addition to the content of the video, which is precisely the challenge that should be addressed by the model. Figure 5 supports this point: GPT-4o-mini showed high classification performance for videos from North American companies, while DeepSeek performed better for videos from Asia. We look forward to future research using our dataset to address these challenges.


> Imbalanced labels affect model performance Labels such as “Patriotism” and “Green Innovation” appear infrequently in the dataset, making it difficult for the model to learn on these labels and resulting in poor prediction performance, especially in the zero-shot setting.

We understand that low-resource labels are challenging for model predictions (and also for evaluation). To address this, we believe it would be valuable to include more videos from different cultures in future work. We will also consider continuously updating the dataset and adding new video sets.


We sincerely thank you for your comments. If you have any concerns or additional comments, please feel free to let us know.

Thank you so much for reviewing and your valuable feedback which helps us improve our submission even further. We believe the main concern in this review centers on the clarity and accessibility of the paper. Please rest assured that this will be addressed in the revised version. Please find more detailed comments addressing your review below.

> While the domain seems novel to me, the task of detection itself is easy, and it is difficult to assess weather a novel algorithm design is needed.

The domain of climate disinformation is a rapidly evolving and socially critical area. While detection tasks in more traditional domains may be well-understood, climate disinformation presents unique challenges that complicate straightforward application of existing methods. 

Our dataset spans diverse cultural and linguistic contexts, contains many low-resource and subtle labels that reflect complex misinformation narratives and includes videos of widely varying lengths (from 10 seconds to over 400 seconds). These factors create substantial barriers for current vision-language models, as reflected in the uneven F1 scores across categories.

Our benchmark aims to support the AI community—including those new to this domain—in developing and evaluating methods capable of addressing these real-world, high-impact challenges. We believe that advancing AI approaches in this space is crucial for tackling misinformation at scale and holds significant societal value.


> The dataset comes with transcripts and visual data, where it is not indicated if the transcripts are obtained by collectors or generated automatically on the framework.

We describe this on Line 131-132: "We transcribe the videos using a speech-to-text model (i.e., Whisper-1 [37]) to create the transcript text in the experiments."


> The scope and size of the dataset seems to be limited, which makes proper evaluation difficult. Note that the domain is new to me, thus, I am not familiar with the scope of the task and available data. This is still a good initiative.

We thank the reviewer for appreciating the initiative and spirit of our submission. We specifically intend this to be an evaluation dataset, and we note that, to date, there are no available resources for multi-modal greenwashing detection. In fact, there is limited availability of datasets for multi-modal analysis more broadly across all climate change domains. Even though it is not directly related to our work, MultiClimate [1], for example, is a recent dataset on climate stance detection from videos, containing a total of 100 videos. In terms of the number of videos, our dataset provides a reasonable sample size (i.e., 692 videos).

We note that our work is comparable to most other evaluation papers. As a rule of thumb, these typically contain a few hundred labeled examples. However, we agree with the reviewer that our benchmark is unlikely to be suitable for fine-tuning models on this task.

More importantly, however, our work is aimed at covering a diverse set of videos rather than a large number of videos. Our work is characterized by fine-grained labels across two different domains: Facebook and YouTube. Moreover, within each domain, we consider a variety of entities. Our dataset covers more than 50 companies and 9 advocacy groups across 21 countries. This makes our benchmark as comprehensive and representative as possible.

We will include the above discussion in the final version of the paper. 
[1] Jiawen Wang et al., MultiClimate: Multimodal Stance Detection on Climate Change Videos, Third Workshop on NLP for Positive Impact.

> The proposed baseline framework seems much more complicated than a benchmark for a simple classification task.

We provide both. In Table 2 (top), we show simple baseline results obtained with zero-shot prompting—without using the proposed baseline framework. However, we note that the 1-shot version usually achieves much better results (except for GPT-4.1). Moreover, to the best of our knowledge, our approach of splitting the videos into frame images and using the transcript along with them is fairly standard for most video classification tasks.

> The details of collection and refining the data seems could benefit from more elaboration and proper human validation.

We want to emphasize that both the dataset and the methods were developed through a multi-stage process involving extensive consultation with domain stakeholders, careful annotation design, and multiple rounds of validation. The details of dataset development can be found in Appendix A.5.4, for example. But we appreciate the comment and will revise our paper to better communicate this process and provide clearer descriptions of our methodology, including adding details described in the appendix into the main part.
We hope these improvements will convey the depth and care that went into the work. We also note that the dataset reflects input from community organisations such as climate NGOs, and we aim for it to serve as a lasting resource. We will ensure this is more clearly reflected in the revised version.

> Overall the paper and dataset seems somehow completed in a rush.

We appreciate the reviewer's feedback regarding the paper’s presentation. We will will improve the manuscript’s clarity, readability, and overall polish in the revision to better reflect the thoroughness of our work.

Again, we thank you for your valuable feedback which helps us improve our paper. If you have any other concerns or comments, please let us know.

summary.value:
This paper introduces a multimodal benchmark dataset for detecting frames and potential greenwashing in oil and gas video ads on Facebook and YouTube. The dataset contains 691 videos annotated with 13 frame types (e.g., environment, community, green innovation), covering more than 50 companies in 21 countries.
The benchmark dataset evaluates the effectiveness of visual language models (VLMs) such as GPT-4.1 and Qwen2.5-VL in zero-shot and one-shot settings. GPT-4.1 achieves the best performance (up to 71% F1 score). Key challenges include detecting implicit frames, handling short videos, and coping with cultural differences.
This work supports automatic greenwashing detection, temporal trend analysis, and deeper research on corporate climate messaging.

strengths_contributions.value:
The first multimodal benchmark for detecting framing and greenwashing in oil and gas video ads.

Expert-annotated dataset of 691 videos from 21 countries and over 50 entities.

Evaluates top VLMs (e.g. GPT-4.1) on multi-label classification of PR messages.

Supports greenwash detection, trend analysis, and corporate profiling.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. Limited label accuracy (especially for the Facebook subset)
Facebook videos are labeled based on ad text rather than the overall content of the video. This “distant annotation” approach may ignore visual and tone cues in the video, reduce annotation quality, and bias model training and evaluation.

2. Difficulty identifying implicit expressions and cultural differences
Many “green” messages in videos are conveyed through metaphors and symbolic images (such as wind power generation, laboratories, etc.) and lack explicit language descriptions. Current models are weak in handling these implicit frames and cross-cultural expression differences (such as Asia vs. North America).

3. Imbalanced labels affect model performance
Labels such as “Patriotism” and “Green Innovation” appear infrequently in the dataset, making it difficult for the model to learn on these labels and resulting in poor prediction performance, especially in the zero-shot setting.

summary.value: This paper proposes a multimodal benchmark dataset for analyzing framing strategies and greenwashing in oil and gas video advertisements. The dataset consists of expert-annotated video ads collected from Facebook and YouTube, covering 13 framing categories across more than 50 companies in 21 countries or regions. The authors conduct experiments in both zero-shot and one-shot settings using multiple vision-language models and report that these models show limited performance on implicit, subtle, and low-resource categories. The proposed dataset serves as a benchmark for the study of framing in oil and gas advertising and greenwashing detection.

strengths_contributions.value:
- This paper introduces the first multimodal annotated dataset for oil and gas advertisements, incorporating video, visual content, and transcribed text to facilitate the evaluation and development of vision-language models.
- The dataset comprises 306 Facebook videos and 386 YouTube videos, covering 5,710 transcribed text segments with broad temporal and geographical diversity. It also includes 13 fine-grained framing labels annotated by domain experts.
- The authors conduct comprehensive zero-shot and one-shot evaluations across six state-of-the-art vision-language models, effectively demonstrating the complexity and difficulty of the proposed benchmark.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- Although the proposed dataset is a valuable contribution in the multimodal domain, its overall scale (692 videos) remains limited compared to prior text-only benchmarks. The relatively small dataset size raises concerns about potential overfitting during fine-tuning, which may partly explain why the authors focus exclusively on zero-shot and one-shot evaluations. This limitation could affect the model’s generalization capability in real-world scenarios.
- While the motivation for a multimodal framework is clear, the absence of unimodal baselines (e.g., text-only classification results) makes it difficult to assess the specific contribution of each modality to the overall performance. Including such comparisons would strengthen the empirical analysis, help validate the added value of the multimodal approach, and substantiate the necessity of constructing a multimodal dataset for this task.
- Despite the use of expert annotations, certain framing categories (e.g., "Green Innovation" vs. "Environment") may suffer from semantic overlap and subjective interpretation. This potential ambiguity may introduce additional uncertainty in model evaluation, particularly when assessing fine-grained framing categories.

Each piece of data contains the video id, video url, annotated labels, video length, and necessary prompts. Running scripts for reproduction are also provided.

summary.value: This paper presents a novel dataset for multimodal framing detection in oil and gas (O&G) corporate advertising, with potential applications in greenwashing detection and strategic communication analysis. The dataset comprises expert-annotated Facebook and YouTube video ads, covering both visual and transcript modalities. It enables the evaluation of vision-language models (VLMs) in zero-shot and few-shot settings. Both the paper and the accompanying dataset documentation are well-written, clearly structured, and accessible, making the benchmark practical and useful for researchers across disciplines.

strengths_contributions.value:
* This is a novel and timely multimodal dataset designed to analyze framing in corporate oil & gas (O&G) video advertisements. It supports potential applications in greenwashing detection and strategic communication analysis, enabling multidisciplinary research across AI, media studies, and climate policy.

* It effectively spans two popular platforms (i.e., Facebook and YouTube), with distinct content styles and audience dynamics, allowing for robust evaluation across diverse media environments.

* The dataset includes 1.2k expert annotations across 691 videos from over 50 entities in 21 countries, offering strong coverage in terms of both geographic and industry diversity.

* Both the paper and accompanying dataset documentation are clearly written, well-structured, and accessible, making it easy for researchers to understand and apply the benchmark.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
* While the dataset construction and labeling process is discussed and grounded in prior work, the paper would benefit from including representative examples to illustrate the label definitions in more detail, helping readers better understand the annotation criteria.

* There are two notable limitations in the Facebook subset: (i) approximately 55% of the videos lack transcripts, reducing the effectiveness of multimodal analysis; and (ii) the data is geographically limited to the United States, which may restrict the generalizability and global relevance of the findings derived from this subset.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

ethical_comments.value: While the paper addresses sensitive topics such as framing manipulation and greenwashing, the dataset itself poses minimal ethical risk as it contains no personal or sensitive information, and all video content is sourced from publicly available ads.

dataset_code_comments.value:
* The dataset is hosted on Kaggle with metadata files provided.

* Documentation is available.

additional_feedback.value: Including representive examples of annotator/labeling would enhance the reader’s understanding of label ambiguity and subjectivity.

final_justification.value: Thanks to the authors for their response and the efforts made to further revise the paper. I am satisfied with their revisions and responses, and I maintain my rating -- recommend acceptance of the paper.

title.value: A Multimodal Benchmark for Framing of Oil & Gas Advertising and Potential Greenwashing Detection

TLDR.value: A benchmark dataset of oil and gas video ads

abstract.value:
Companies spend large amounts of money on public relations campaigns to project a positive brand image.
However, sometimes there is a mismatch between what they say and what they do. Oil & gas companies, for example, are accused of "greenwashing" with imagery of climate-friendly initiatives.
Understanding the framing, and changes in framing, at scale can help better understand the goals and nature of public relation campaigns.
To address this, we introduce a benchmark dataset of expert-annotated video ads obtained from Facebook and YouTube.
The dataset provides annotations for 13 framing types for more than 50 companies or advocacy groups across 20 countries.
Our dataset is especially designed for the evaluation of vision-language models (VLMs), distinguishing it from past text-only framing datasets.
Baseline experiments show some promising results, while leaving room for improvement for future work: GPT-4.1 can detect environmental messages with 79% F1 score, while our best model only achieves 46% F1 score on identifying framing around green innovation.
We also identify challenges that VLMs must address, such as implicit framing, handling  videos of various lengths, or implicit cultural backgrounds.
Our dataset contributes to research in multimodal analysis of strategic communication in the energy sector.
